Newborn Care

Using acetaminophen for teething pain: comfort, dosing checks and warning signs

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A chilled teether or a cuddle may be enough for some babies, while others seem more uncomfortable as a tooth comes through. Acetaminophen (also called paracetamol) can help with pain when it is appropriate for the child and used correctly. The goal is short-term comfort with a clear medicine plan, not continuous dosing through all the months in which teeth appear.

Teething discomfort varies from baby to baby

A tooth emerging through the gum can cause soreness, pressure or an urge to chew. Some babies have little trouble; others are more unsettled for a few days. We cannot know exactly how a baby describes the sensation, so there is no need to decide whether it counts as pain or itching before offering comfort.

The first tooth often appears around six months, but timing varies widely. Starting to drool or chew does not prove that a tooth is the cause of every new symptom. Assess how your baby is feeding, responding and behaving overall, rather than treating teething as a diagnosis that explains everything.

Look for a pattern, not one isolated sign

Tender or red gums, extra drool and chewing can fit teething. Your baby may want more cuddles, seem fretful, rub an ear or sleep less well. Ear pulling and clinginess are nonspecific: they can also occur for reasons unrelated to a tooth.

Notice whether your baby can be comforted and still takes feeds and has their usual wet nappies. Persistent severe crying, marked feeding changes or a child who seems ill deserves a fresh assessment. Do not assume that louder crying means a larger medicine dose is needed.

A true fever needs a different explanation

Teething may coincide with a slight temperature rise, but a temperature of 38°C or above should not simply be attributed to it. Significant diarrhoea is not an established teething symptom either. Use a thermometer rather than deciding from warm cheeks alone.

A baby younger than three months with a temperature of 38°C or higher needs urgent medical assessment. At any age, difficulty breathing, being very hard to wake, a seizure or a seriously unwell appearance needs urgent or emergency help. Pain relief must not delay finding out what is wrong.

Try gum comfort and supervised chewing

Wash your hands and gently massage the sore gum with a clean finger. Offer a suitable firm teething ring and follow its cleaning and chilling instructions. Refrigeration can help if the product permits it; freezing can make the surface hard enough to hurt the gum. Check for damage before use and supervise chewing.

A clean, cool damp cloth may be soothing when you hold and supervise it. Do not leave cloths or teethers in the sleep space or attach them around the neck. An age-appropriate baby toothbrush is for supervised oral care, not something to leave a baby chewing alone. Cuddling and play can help too.

Food can soothe only when the baby is ready for it

If your baby has already started complementary foods, an appropriately prepared cool, soft food can be another comfort option. Keep the texture suited to their feeding skills and supervise closely. Teething is not a reason to start solids before the baby is developmentally ready.

Do not offer hard frozen food, small choking hazards or sugary snacks as a pain treatment. Continue normal breast or formula feeds and seek advice if intake falls. Wipe dribble gently rather than repeatedly rubbing the skin, which can become sore.

When acetaminophen may be reasonable

If gum discomfort remains troublesome despite comfort measures, ask whether acetaminophen is suitable. For children under two, the American Academy of Pediatrics advises using it with a doctor’s guidance. Local labels and recommendations differ, so being over three months old is not a universal permission to choose a dose yourself.

Have the baby’s age, current weight, health conditions and exact medicine bottle available. Ask whether the symptoms fit teething, which preparation to use, how long to use it and when to call again. Tell the clinician about any other medicine already given, including products from another country.

Check concentration before thinking in millilitres

The amount of medicine and the volume of liquid are different. A label such as 160 mg/5 mL describes concentration, not a dose for every baby. US children’s liquid commonly uses that strength, while Health Canada lists infant drops containing 80 mg/mL and NHS guidance describes a UK infant liquid containing 120 mg/5 mL.

The same number of millilitres can therefore contain very different amounts of acetaminophen. Do not use an online weight-to-volume shortcut, another child’s instructions or a remembered dose from an old bottle. Ask for the dose in millilitres for the precise concentration you have. Chewable, dissolving and adult products are not interchangeable with infant drops.

Confirm the interval and daily maximum too

A safe plan includes the amount per dose, the shortest permitted interval, the maximum in twenty-four hours and the point at which symptoms need review. A label allowing repeated doses does not mean your child needs every permitted dose. Do not give another early because the first has not yet seemed to work.

Guidance differs: the AAP’s US instructions allow no more than five doses in twenty-four hours, while NHS directions for common child preparations usually allow four, with different rules for very young babies. Follow the instructions confirmed for your child and product, rather than choosing whichever maximum is larger.

Measure, record and coordinate with other caregivers

Use the supplied oral syringe or one a pharmacist has confirmed is suitable, and read the millilitre markings carefully. A household teaspoon is not an accurate measuring tool. Follow any shaking instructions. Having a device in the box does not prevent a mistake if its markings or the prescribed amount are misunderstood.

Record the amount and time immediately and tell the next caregiver. Check every medicine for duplicate acetaminophen or paracetamol: those are two names for the same drug. Replace the cap and store the medicine out of reach and sight. Recheck the concentration whenever you open a new bottle.

Night-time relief is different from using a sleep medicine

Pain may make it harder to settle, and appropriate pain relief may help when discomfort is the reason. That does not make acetaminophen a sleep aid. Avoid a standing dose before every nap or every night simply because teeth are expected to emerge.

If bedtime discomfort is recurrent, discuss the pattern and a short-term plan rather than adopting a universal “one hour before bed” rule. Continue ordinary soothing and safe sleep practices. Ongoing need for medicine, or sleep disruption that persists without clear gum discomfort, calls for review rather than indefinite treatment.

How does ibuprofen compare?

Ibuprofen is another pain reliever, but it has different eligibility and safety considerations. US AAP advice is not to use it below six months without a doctor’s direction; some UK preparations can be used younger under their specific age and weight rules. One country’s age cutoff is not an international dosing instruction.

Hydration, stomach or kidney problems, other medicines and the child’s health affect the choice. Avoid ibuprofen in a dehydrated child unless the treating clinician directs otherwise. There is no need to claim one medicine is always best or that the two always work equally well for every baby. Do not alternate them without a clear professional plan.

Avoid risky teething shortcuts

Do not use amber necklaces or other teething jewellery: pieces can choke a child and cords can strangle. Avoid numbing products containing benzocaine or lidocaine for infant teething; these can cause serious harm and offer little useful relief. A product sold for the mouth or described as natural is not automatically suitable for a baby.

Homeopathic teething tablets and similar remedies are not a reliable substitute for evidence-based care. Advice about particular locally licensed products can vary, so ask a pharmacist about the exact ingredient rather than borrowing an adult mouth gel. Safer comfort measures should remain the starting point.

Know when to call and what to do after a possible dosing error

Contact the child’s clinician if pain seems severe, medicine is not helping, repeated doses are needed, feeding is reduced or you are unsure what is happening. Bring the bottle and dosing record. You can ask for help even when there is no emergency; uncertainty is a reasonable reason to call.

If too much acetaminophen may have been given, contact your local poison service or urgent medical care immediately, even if the child looks well. Serious liver injury may not be obvious at first. Keep the packaging and the times and amounts available. Do not give further doses while waiting for professional advice.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Teething can cause local gum discomfort, but fever, significant illness or persistent severe distress should not be explained away as a tooth coming through. Comfort measures and symptom review belong alongside any medicine decision.

Acetaminophen instructions depend on age, weight, concentration and local product labelling. Comparing current US, Canadian and UK guidance shows why a single international millilitre chart or daily maximum would be misleading.

How BeMama can help

Keep a simple shared note with the exact product strength, confirmed dose, time given and the next permitted time. This makes handovers easier when several people care for a tired or uncomfortable baby.

When to seek help

Seek urgent assessment for a temperature of 38°C or more in a baby under three months. Breathing difficulty, marked unresponsiveness or a seizure requires emergency help. For a possible overdose, contact poison control or urgent care immediately rather than waiting for symptoms.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Teething symptoms are variable; fever and an unwell baby need assessment.
  • Start with supervised gum comfort and appropriate chilled, never frozen, teethers.
  • Confirm the exact concentration, millilitre dose, interval and daily maximum.
  • Record doses and check other medicines for the same active ingredient.
  • Repeated pain, poor feeding or possible overdose needs professional advice.

Frequently asked questions

Are acetaminophen and paracetamol different medicines?

No. They are two names for the same active ingredient. Do not combine products on the assumption that the different names make them separate painkillers.

Is 160 mg/5 mL the amount every teething baby should receive?

No. It is a concentration. The dose depends on the child and the exact product, and other concentrations are sold internationally.

Can I reuse the millilitre dose from another bottle?

Only after confirming that the product and professional instructions match. Similar packaging does not prove the same strength, and infant drops may be more concentrated.

Is five doses in a day always allowed?

No. Daily limits differ by product, age and local guidance. Use the limit confirmed for your child; do not choose a larger maximum from another country’s website.

Can teething explain a temperature of 38°C?

Do not assume so. A true fever needs consideration of illness, and a baby under three months with that temperature needs urgent assessment.

Should I give medicine before every bedtime while teeth are coming in?

No. It is for appropriate short-term pain relief, not routine sleep promotion. Persistent night-time discomfort needs review and an individualized plan.

Can I switch to ibuprofen or alternate medicines?

Ask whether it is suitable for your child’s age, weight and hydration. Do not alternate without clear instructions about amounts and times.

Can I freeze a teething ring for stronger relief?

No. A frozen surface can injure the gums. Follow the product’s refrigeration instructions and supervise use.

Are natural teething necklaces or gels safer?

No. Jewellery creates choking and strangulation risks, while some numbing or homeopathic products can be harmful. Check the exact product with a pharmacist.

What if two caregivers may have both given a dose?

Get prompt advice from poison control or urgent care, with the bottle and possible amounts/times. Do not wait for symptoms or give more while the situation is being assessed.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
